head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: An odd total can never split into two equal halves
A bitset stored in one Python integer: bit `s` is 1 iff some subset sums to `s`
Subset-sum reachability; Python ints are arbitrary size
Only the empty subset (sum 0) is reachable at first
Shifts every reachable sum up by `x`, i.e. 'take x into the subset'
Adding one item to all subsets at once
Keep old sums (skip x) and add the new ones (take x)
Is the half-sum reachable? (`>>` binds tighter than `&`)

p: `[1,5,11,5]`, total 22, so the target is 11. The string shows bits for sums 22 down to 0 (rightmost = sum 0):

blocks.h: Why a bitset instead of a boolean DP (Dynamic Programming) array?
p: The classic DP loops over `x` and then over sums in reverse: O(n · target) bit-by-bit operations. A shift-and-or does all sums for one item in a single big-integer operation, which runs about 64 sums per machine word.

blocks.h: Why is the 0/1 constraint safe here?
p: Each item is shifted once from the OLD `bits` value (the right side is evaluated before the OR), so an item can't be used twice. That is why the loop in the array version goes from high sums to low.

bullets: Time: O(n · total / w) with word size w, in practice very fast.

416.takeaway: Partition equal subset sum is subset-sum to total/2; a Python big-int bitset does the knapsack DP with `bits |= bits << x`.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: No ship cell directly above (or the top row, which also guards the index)
No ship cell directly to the left
count only the top-left cell of each ship
Ships are straight lines, so each has exactly one cell with nothing above and nothing left
Count heads instead of running a flood fill

p: Board `X..X / ...X / ...X`:

A flood fill marks cells visited (mutating the board or using O(mn) extra space). Because ships are guaranteed to be straight and separated, checking just up and left identifies each ship's first cell with no extra memory.

If ships could touch (be adjacent), a cell could have a ship above and another beside, and the head test would miscount. The problem promises at least one cell of separation, which is what makes the shortcut valid.

419.takeaway: Battleships: count each ship once by counting only cells with no ship above or to the left; one pass and O(1) space, thanks to ships being straight and separated.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Each node is written as `value childCount`
A count prefix makes the format self-delimiting: no brackets or null markers needed
Pre-order: a node is written before its children
Pre-order + counts uniquely determines a tree
A one-shot iterator over the tokens; `next(it)` consumes one at a time
Parsing recursively without passing an index around
Read exactly `k` children by calling `build` k times
The count tells the parser when to stop

p: Tree `1` with children `3` (children `5`, `6`), `2`, `4` serialises to `"1 3 3 2 5 0 6 0 2 0 4 0"`. Reading it left to right as pairs:

blocks.h: Why a child count instead of markers?
p: With a binary tree you can write `null` for a missing child. An N-ary node has any number of children, so a terminator or a count is needed. A count is shorter, and the parser can simply loop `k` times; brackets would need depth tracking.
Recursion consumes the token list from the left. A shared iterator advances automatically across recursive calls, so no `index` variable has to be threaded or kept in a `nonlocal`.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the string and O(h) recursion.

428.takeaway: Serialise an N-ary tree in pre-order with `value childCount`; the counts make decoding a simple recursive read.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sum from the ROOT down to the current node (a prefix sum along the path)
Prefix sums turn 'sum of a subpath' into a subtraction
How many ancestors on the current path have each prefix sum; starts with `{0: 1}` for the empty prefix above the root
Counting earlier prefix values on the path
Number of ancestors `a` whose prefix equals `cur - target`: each gives a downward path summing to exactly `target`
The same idea as Subarray Sum Equals K, on a tree path
The current node becomes available as a prefix for its descendants
Remove it when leaving, so siblings don't see it
Backtracking: the dictionary must only reflect the current root-to-node path

p: Tree `[10,5,-3,3,2,null,11]`, `target = 8`. Each row is a node visited (pre-order): its prefix sum and how many paths ending here sum to 8.
`5 → 3` (prefix 18 matches the earlier prefix 10 at the root: 18 - 10 = 8) and `-3 → 11` (prefix 18 minus the prefix 10 again). The answer is 2.

The dictionary is shared by the whole recursion. If a left subtree's prefix sums stayed in it, a node in the right subtree could pair with a value that is not its ancestor, counting paths that don't exist.

head: Approach
Time
Space
rows: DFS (Depth-First Search) from every node, brute force
O(n²) worst, O(n log n) balanced

bullets: Space: O(h) for recursion and the map.

437.takeaway: Count downward paths with sum k using prefix sums along the root-to-node path: a Counter of ancestor prefixes, decremented on exit.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Scans the input, one whole run at a time
Position where the compressed output is written; always ≤ `read`, so it never overwrites unread characters
The compressed form keeps one copy
Writes each DIGIT of the count as its own character (`12` becomes `'1','2'`)
The problem wants single-character list items
A run of length 1 is written without a number

blocks.h: Why is writing in place safe?
p: Each run needs at most as many output characters as input characters (a run of length L ≥ 2 writes 1 letter plus the digits of L, which is never more than L characters). So `write` never passes `read`, and unread input is never overwritten.

bullets: Space: O(1), the list is rewritten in place and the new length is returned.

443.takeaway: In-place run-length encoding with a read pointer for runs and a write pointer for output; counts ≥ 10 are written digit by digit.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sort balloons by their RIGHT end
Interval problems: sorting by end is the greedy order for 'fewest points that hit every interval'
Position of the last arrow fired (starts at -∞)
This balloon starts after the last arrow: it is not hit, so a new arrow is needed
Fire the new arrow at this balloon's right end
As far right as possible while still hitting it, to catch the most later balloons
Smaller than any coordinate, so the first balloon always needs an arrow

blocks.h: Why sort by END and shoot at the end?
p: Among balloons not yet burst, the one that ends first limits where an arrow can go. Firing at its right end hits it and reaches as far right as possible, so it bursts every other balloon that overlaps that point. Any other position for this arrow can only hit a subset of those balloons.
Use `s > end`, not `>=`: balloons that merely touch (`[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) share the point 2, so one arrow handles both.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.

452.takeaway: Fewest arrows = interval stabbing: sort by right end and greedily shoot at the end of the first uncovered balloon.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sort greed factors and cookie sizes ascending
Greedy matching needs both sides ordered
Index of the least greedy child still unfed
Also the answer: how many children are content
Try cookies from smallest to largest
This cookie satisfies the least greedy remaining child
Give it to them, move to the next child

blocks.h: Why match the smallest cookie to the least greedy child?
p: A small cookie can only satisfy a small greed, so offering it to the smallest unmet child wastes nothing; a big cookie then remains available for greedier children. If a cookie is too small for even the least greedy child, it is useless to everyone remaining, so it is skipped.

head: Strategy
Risk
rows: Give biggest cookie to the greediest child
may waste cookies on children who would be fine with less
Smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy child (this code)

bullets: Time: O(n log n + m log m) for the sorts; the matching pass is O(m).

455.takeaway: Assign cookies: sort both, sweep the cookies, and give each to the least greedy unfed child it satisfies.

Comparing two numbers bit by bit
Quick way to see the bits (the prefix `0b` has no `1`s so counting is safe)

p: Interviewers often want the Kernighan loop (problem 191); the built-in form is fine when the language allows it.
Hamming distance is the number of positions where the bits differ. XOR yields 1 exactly there and 0 where they agree, so the distance is the popcount of the XOR.

bullets: Time: O(log max(x, y)), proportional to the number of bits.
Space: O(log max(x, y)) for the temporary string.

461.takeaway: Hamming distance = popcount of x XOR y.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A bitmask of the numbers already taken: bit `i` set means `i + 1` is used
Small sets (≤ 20 items) as DP (Dynamic Programming) state
Can the player to move force a win with these numbers left and `total` still needed?
Picking `i + 1` reaches or passes the target: immediate win
Pick `i + 1`, then the OPPONENT must be in a losing state
The win condition for minimax: you win if some move leaves the opponent losing
At most 2^m masks (`total` is determined by `used`)
Even using every number nobody can reach the target: nobody wins
Early exit; also avoids an endless game

p: Quick checks against the code:

head: maxChoosable, target
Result
Why
States memoised
rows: no first move forces a win (the search finds none)
the search finds a first move that forces a win

blocks.h: Why is `used` enough as the cache key?
p: `total` is `desiredTotal` minus the sum of the used numbers, so it follows from `used`. The key `(used, total)` stays correct but only `used` varies, so the state space is at most 2^m (about 1 million for m = 20) instead of 2^m × target.

The player to move wins if ANY move either reaches the target or leaves the opponent in a position the opponent loses. Because both play optimally, a position is losing exactly when every move leaves the opponent winning; the loop returns `False` only after trying all of them.

464.takeaway: Can I Win: minimax over a bitmask of used numbers with memoisation; you win if some move wins now or leaves the opponent losing.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Given API (Application Programming Interface): uniform integers 1..7
Two rolls form a base-7 number: the first picks a row of 7, the second a column. Result is uniform over 1..49
Combining two uniform draws into a bigger uniform range
Accept only 1..40, a multiple of 10; reject 41..49 and roll again
Rejection sampling keeps the distribution uniform
Folding a uniform range that is a multiple of 10

p: Each output 1..10 receives exactly four of the 40 accepted values:

49 outcomes are not divisible by 10. Using all of them with `% 10` would give digits 1..9 five chances each and 0 only four, making them unequal. Throwing away the 9 extra outcomes makes the remaining 40 split evenly.

Each attempt succeeds with probability 40/49, so the expected number of attempts is 49/40 ≈ 1.225, i.e. about 2.45 calls to `rand7()` per `rand10()`. The worst case has no bound, but the chance of many rejections decays geometrically.

470.takeaway: Rejection sampling: build a uniform range from rand7 (two draws → 1..49), reject the tail that doesn't divide evenly, and fold what's left.

Extend the run on a 1, reset on a 0 (`x` is truthy for 1)
Update after every element so a run ending at the array's end is counted

p: If you only updated when a 0 appears, an array ending with 1s (like this one) would lose its last run. Taking the max on every step needs no special final check.

485.takeaway: Longest run of 1s: a running counter that resets on 0, with the max updated every step.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Dict: running sum → number of sign assignments so far that produce it
DP (Dynamic Programming) keyed by value, sparse instead of a big array
One way to make sum 0 with no numbers
`nxt[k] += c` works without checking `k` is present
Each existing sum splits into two: add `x` or subtract `x`
Count for the target, or 0 if no assignment reaches it

p: `nums = [1,1,1,1,1]`, `target = 3`. Sums reachable after each number, with how many ways:

blocks.h: Why a dict and not a full array?
p: The sums range from -total to +total but only some are reachable at a time, and many collide (e.g. +1 -1 and -1 +1 both give 0). The dict merges all assignments that reach the same sum, so the number of states stays at most 2·total + 1 instead of 2ⁿ paths.
Five assignments reach 3: choose which one of the five 1s is subtracted (4 plus, 1 minus gives 3).

bullets: Time: O(n · S) where S is the sum of the numbers.

494.takeaway: Target sum: DP over a dictionary of reachable sums, branching ±x at each step and merging equal sums.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of integer points in a rectangle (edges inclusive)
Weighting by area so every POINT is equally likely
Running totals (prefix sums) of the areas
Index of the first prefix sum greater than `r`: the rectangle owning ticket `r`
Binary search in O(log n) over the sorted prefix list
Uniform point inside the chosen rectangle

p: Rectangles `[-2,-2,1,1]` (4×4 = 16 points) and `[2,2,4,6]` (3×5 = 15 points) give prefix sums [16, 31]. A ticket `r` in 0..30 belongs to the first rectangle if `r < 16`:

blocks.h: Why choose the rectangle by weight?
p: Picking a rectangle uniformly would make points in small rectangles more likely than points in big ones. Weighting by point count gives every integer point probability 1/total: P(rect) × P(point | rect) = (area/total) × (1/area).

Ticket 16 is the first ticket of the second rectangle, and `pre[0] = 16`. `bisect_right` returns 1 for 16 (it places `r` after equal values), so ticket 16 maps to rectangle 1; `bisect_left` would wrongly give rectangle 0.

bullets: Time: O(log n) per `pick`; O(n) to build.
Space: O(n) for the prefix sums.

497.takeaway: Uniform point over several rectangles: pick a rectangle with probability proportional to its point count (prefix sums + bisect), then a uniform point inside it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Stack of INDICES whose next greater element is not found yet; values are non-increasing from bottom to top
Walk the array twice to simulate the circle
Circular array: unroll by iterating `2n` with `i % n`
Value at the current position on either lap
`while st and nums[st[-1]] < x: ans[st.pop()] = x`
`x` is the next greater element for every smaller one waiting on the stack
Resolve all pending smaller elements at once
Only push on the first lap; the second lap only resolves leftovers
Avoids pushing duplicates and keeps the stack size ≤ n
Elements never resolved have no greater element anywhere

p: On the first lap the last elements cannot see the beginning of the array. The second lap offers the early values as candidates for elements still on the stack. In this example the last `1` (index 2) finds `2` on the second lap, which a single pass would miss.

head: Approach
Time
Space
rows: Brute force: for each i scan the circle

blocks.h: Why is it O(n) despite the nested loop?
p: Each index is pushed once (during the first lap) and popped at most once, so the inner `while` runs at most n times in total across all `2n` iterations.

503.takeaway: Next greater element in a circular array: monotonic stack of indices over two laps (`i % n`), pushing only on the first lap.

Simultaneous assignment: the right side is fully evaluated first, then both names update
Advancing a two-term recurrence without a temp variable
Applies the step `n` times; `a` ends as `F(n)`
Why the loop runs n and not n-1 times

p: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` recomputes the same values exponentially often. Iterating keeps only the last two values.

509.takeaway: Fibonacci with two rolling variables and tuple assignment: O(n) time, O(1) space; mention fast doubling for O(log n).

rows: Queue seeded with the root; empty tree gives an empty queue
At the start of each round the queue holds exactly one whole level, so its max is that level's max
Level-order BFS (Breadth-First Search): the queue IS the level
Pop exactly the current level's nodes and enqueue their children

p: DFS with a `depth` argument and `res[depth] = max(res[depth], val)` also works in O(n) time and O(h) space. BFS reads naturally for 'per level' questions and the code above needs no depth variable.

bullets: Space: O(w) for the queue, where w is the maximum width.

515.takeaway: Per-level aggregates = level-order BFS where the queue at the start of each round is exactly one level.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of combinations of the coins processed so far that sum to `a`
One way to make 0 (use no coins)
Introduce one coin type at a time
Each combination is counted in one canonical order (by coin type)
Forward order lets the SAME coin be reused in the same pass
Add the combinations that end with one more coin `c`

p: `amount = 5`, `coins = [1,2,5]`; `dp` indexed 0..5 after each coin type:

blocks.h: Why coins in the OUTER loop?
p: Looping coins outside fixes the order in which coin types are considered, so `1+2` and `2+1` are the same combination and counted once. Putting the amount outside (as in Combination Sum IV) counts sequences, so `1+2` and `2+1` count twice.
Going from `c` upward, `dp[a - c]` has already been updated with this coin, so the coin can be used again. Going downward (0/1 knapsack) would allow each coin once.

518.takeaway: Coin Change II (count combinations): coins in the outer loop, amounts ascending in the inner loop.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Visits BST (Binary Search Tree) values in ascending order
The previously visited value; `None` before the first visit
Compare each value with its predecessor
Lets the inner function rebind the outer variables
In sorted order the smallest difference must be between ADJACENT values, and the difference is non-negative

p: In a sorted sequence, for any two values `a < c` with something `b` between them, `b - a` and `c - b` are both smaller than `c - a`. So the closest pair is always neighbours in sorted order, and the in-order walk produces exactly those pairs.

530.takeaway: Min difference in a BST: an in-order traversal gives sorted values, so only consecutive differences matter; keep the previous value.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Shared cursor into the string; every recursive call advances it
Reads a whole number, including a minus sign and multiple digits
Create the node from the digits just read
Step over `(`, parse the child, step over `)`
Each pair of brackets wraps one child
A second bracket group is the RIGHT child; a single group is always the LEFT child
Empty string means an empty tree

p: `"4(2(3)(1))(6(5))"`. Each row is a call to `parse` (depth = recursion depth) and where the cursor is afterwards:

blocks.h: Why is a single bracket group the left child?
p: The format only writes the right child when a left child exists. So after the value, the first `(…)` is the left subtree and an optional second `(…)` is the right subtree: `4(2)` has only a left child, never only a right child.

blocks.h: Why do the `i += 1` after a child matter?
p: `parse()` stops right at the child's closing `)`. The extra `i += 1` consumes it so the parent can check whether another `(` follows.

bullets: Time: O(n), the cursor moves forward only.

536.takeaway: Recursive-descent parsing with a shared cursor: read a number, then an optional `(left)` and an optional `(right)`.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Convert `HH:MM` to minutes after midnight (slicing skips the colon)
Order the minutes; the closest pair must be adjacent
Same argument as Minimum Absolute Difference
The wrap-around gap from the latest time to the earliest time the next day (1440 minutes in a day)

p: Time is circular: 23:59 and 00:00 are one minute apart. Sorting puts them at opposite ends of the list, so the pair must be checked explicitly with the first element shifted by a full day.

There are only 1440 distinct minutes. With more than 1440 time points two must be equal, so the answer is 0 immediately; some solutions add `if len(timePoints) > 1440: return 0` (and a bucket array instead of sorting gives O(n + 1440)).

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the minutes list.

539.takeaway: Minimum time difference: convert to minutes, sort, compare neighbours, and include the wrap-around gap between last and first.
